You now have access to some commands to help complete the user's request. You are able to access the user's machine with these commands. In every message you send, include "COMMAND: " with your command at the end. Here is a list of commands with explanations of how they are used:
PYTHON(function.py) - Run a python script with the given file name. Use quotes for the filename argument. Do not use quotes in the function command itself.

When you use a command, the user will respond with "Response: " followed by the output of the commmand. Use this output to help the user complete their request.

Hi, your job is to interpret a function f(x) that is implemented in the ./temp/function.py script. f(x) takes numerical inputs.
All you can do is call f(x) on a value of x by running PYTHON(./temp/function.py value). 
Try to describe the function implemented by f(x) by running experiments on it. 
You can call the function on multiple inputs at a time by running PYTHON(./temp/function.py value1 value2 value3 ...). 
You can run the function multiple times on the same input. We encourage testing a large range of values before writing a description. You can test values between [-128 and 128]. 
The output could be noisy and your goal is to find a good simple description of f(x) that explains most of the function behavior. f(x) may combine multiple different operations.
There may be an interval inside the domain where the function behaves differently. If that is the case, describe that interval.
Your description of the function should have three parts. 
First, [DESCRIPTION]: Describe what the function is doing in language. 
[DOMAIN]: What is the domain of the function? Is there an interval where the function displays unexpected behavior? What are the numeric bounds of that interval? What is going on there?
[CODE]: Write python code that approximates the behavior of the function.

I'll start by exploring the function's behavior across a range of values.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -10 -5 -2 -1 0 1 2 5 10)

Response: -10 -5 -2 -1 0 1 2 5 10

That's interesting - it seems to output the input values for these. Let me try more values and non-integers.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -3.5 -2.5 -1.5 -0.5 0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5)

Response: -3.5 -2.5 -1.5 -0.5 0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5

Still just returning inputs. Let me test extreme values and check if there's some interval where it changes.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -128 -100 -50 -20 20 50 100 128)

Response: -128 -100 -50 -20 20 50 100 128

Still identity. Let me test more carefully with a wide variety and also repeat same value to check for noise.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 0.001 0.01 0.1 0.3 0.7 0.99 1 7 15 30 60 90 120 127)

Response: 0.001 0.01 0.1 0.3 0.7 0.99 1 7 15 30 60 90 120 127

Hmm, all identity so far. Let me try values near some specific points and odd values, and repeat to check noise.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 2 2 3 3 4 4 8 8 16 16 32 32 64 64)

Response: 2 2 3 3 4 4 8 8 16 16 32 32 64 64

Let me try a larger set including negatives and check if maybe there's a threshold somewhere near certain specific values, like powers or e-related.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -64 -32 -16 -8 -4 -2 -1 -0.5 -0.25 0.25 0.5 4 8 16 32 64)

Response: -64 -32 -16 -8 -4 -2 -1 -0.5 -0.25 0.25 0.5 4 8 16 32 64

Everything is identity so far. Let me try some values that might trigger a special branch - maybe very small, or checking specific constants.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 3.14159 2.71828 1.41421 1.61803 100 127 128 -128 -127)

Response: 3.14159 2.71828 1.41421 1.61803 100 127 128 -128 -127

Still identity. This is puzzling. Let me try some values that might be edge cases - maybe near zero with tiny values, or maybe the function has a branch for very specific intervals.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 0 -0 0.0001 -0.0001 1e-5 -1e-5 1e-10 50 -50 75 -75 100 -100)

Response: 0 -0 0.0001 -0.0001 1e-05 -1e-05 1e-10 50 -50 75 -75 100 -100

Everything is coming back as identity. Let me try some more unusual values to detect any branching, like values near 1 and near specific thresholds.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 0.9999 1.0001 0.99999 1.00001 1.5 2.5 3.5 -0.9999 -1.0001)

Response: 0.9999 1.0001 0.99999 1.00001 1.5 2.5 3.5 -0.9999 -1.0001

Let me try much more extreme and test if maybe there's an unusual interval. Let me also try repeated calls on a range to detect randomness.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 5 5 5 10 10 10 20 20 20 40 40 40)

Response: 5 5 5 10 10 10 20 20 20 40 40 40

Consistently identity. Let me try values that might be near a "special" range like [2,4] or around certain integer regions more densely.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 1.1 1.2 1.3 1.4 1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8 1.9 2.1 2.2 2.3 2.4 2.6 2.8 2.9)

Response: 1.1 1.2 1.3 1.4 1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8 1.9 2.1 2.2 2.3 2.4 2.6 2.8 2.9

Let me try some values near 0 in a denser way, and also test very large negative near -128 more thoroughly, maybe there's a clamp or branch hidden somewhere.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -128 -120 -110 -90 -80 -70 -60 -40 -30 -26 -25 -24 -23 -22 -21 -19 -18 -17)

Response: -128 -120 -110 -90 -80 -70 -60 -40 -30 -26 -25 -24 -23 -22 -21 -19 -18 -17

Still identity. Let me try a dense sampling around a few regions to catch anything, and also test decimal precision values that might round.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 0.3333333 0.6666667 1.3333333 1.6666667 2.3333333 2.6666667 12.5 25 37.5 62.5 87.5 112.5)

Response: 0.3333333 0.6666667 1.3333333 1.6666667 2.3333333 2.6666667 12.5 25 37.5 62.5 87.5 112.5

Everything returns identity. Perhaps the function is literally the identity function, but let me test some potentially problematic cases: very large values beyond expected range, and NaN-ish triggers, and negatives near -1.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 200 500 1000 10000 -200 -500 -1000 -10000)

Response: 200 500 1000 10000 -200 -500 -1000 -10000

The function is extending beyond the stated domain too. Let me try a really wide test to be thorough and check for any hidden behavior - including some values that could trigger log, sqrt of negative, etc.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py -1.5 -2 -3 -4 -16 -0.1 -0.2 -0.3 -0.7 -99 -125 99 125 126)

Response: -1.5 -2 -3 -4 -16 -0.1 -0.2 -0.3 -0.7 -99 -125 99 125 126

It appears the function is simply the identity function f(x) = x across all tested values. Let me do one final confirmation with a broad random-looking sample including repeats to ensure no noise.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py 7 13 21 34 55 89 -7 -13 -21 -34 -55 -89 0.75 -0.75 3 3 3)

Response: 7 13 21 34 55 89 -7 -13 -21 -34 -55 -89 0.75 -0.75 3 3 3

The function consistently returns exactly its input for every value I tested across [-128, 128] and beyond, with no noise and no special interval behavior detected.

[DESCRIPTION]: The function f(x) appears to be the identity function. For every input x tested (integers, decimals, negatives, very small values near zero, values near ±1, and values well beyond ±128 up to ±10000), the output equals the input exactly. There is no sign of any transformation, clamping, branching, or noise. The output format simply echoes the inputs back in the same order.

[DOMAIN]: The function accepts all real (and apparently arbitrary-magnitude) numerical inputs. I found no interval where behavior differs from identity; testing between [-128, 128] and beyond (up to ±10000) revealed no unexpected behavior. If there is a special interval, it was not triggered by any of the broad, dense sampling I performed.

[CODE]:
```python
def f(x):
    return x
```

If the real function does have a hidden special interval, my sampling didn't hit it. Based on all evidence, the simplest and most accurate description is f(x) = x.
